senses: Abstinent from alcohol; never drinking alcohol.
Opposed to the drinking of alcohol.
Containing no alcohol.
ety: From total, the reduplicated tee acts as an intensifier, hence T-total. First use appears in 1834.
examples: There is absolutely a teetotal society here in the heart of the mountains, and some quarrelsome drunkards have become reformed!

senses: A flat round pancake-like pastry from Lower Brittany, made with wheat.
A soft thin light fabric with a crinkled surface.
Rubber in sheets, used especially for shoe soles.
A death notice printed on white card with a background of black crepe paper or cloth, placed on the door of a residence or business.
ety: Borrowed from French crêpe, from Latin crispus. Doublet of crisp and crape.
examples: Aside from their pierogis, their menu also includes Ukrainian borscht soup, nalysnyky crepes and uzvar, a traditional drink made out of dried fruits and honey.
The policeman wore crepe-soled shoes.

senses: A white paste, made from ground fish, that is used to make formed and textured food products.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese すり身 (surimi, “ground meat”).
examples: In Singapore, the most popular surimi-based product is the fish ball, which is used in a local application, Yong Tau Foo.

senses: A member of a tribe who works in leather and agriculture; a tanner or leather-worker.
ety: Borrowed from Hindi चमार (camār).
examples: It is not strictly a native patent, though chamars of the skin and hide castes can, if irritated, despatch a Sending which sits on the breast of their enemy by night and nearly kills him.

senses: Freshly green; verdant; covered with verdure, or consisting of it.
Having youthful or new qualities.
ety: Originated c. 1595–1605, verdure + -ous, ultimately from verd (“green”), from Latin viridis.
examples: The hill was blanketed in verdurous grasses.

senses: A place set apart, as with a sanctum sanctorum; a sacred or private place; a private retreat or workroom.
ety: From Latin sānctum (“that which is holy”).
examples: For myself, I had no need to make any change; I should not be called upon to quit my sanctum of the schoolroom; for a sanctum it was now become to me, – "a very pleasant refuge in time of trouble."
A diary, after all, is a sanctum for self-confession.

senses: Encoded or encrypted text.
ety: From cipher + text.
examples: All ciphertexts look alike; that's how you know they're in code.

senses: The trefoil leaf of any small clover, especially Trifolium repens, or such a leaf from a clover-like plant, commonly used as a symbol of Ireland.
ety: From Irish seamróg, from Old Irish semróc, diminutive of semar, semair (“clover”), from Proto-Celtic *semarā, *semaris (compare Gaulish uisumaris (“clover”)), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *semh₁r-, *smeh₁r-. Related to Old Norse smári (“clover”) and possibly Georgian სამყურა (samq̇ura, “clover”).
examples: She wore a shamrock in honor of her Irish ancestry.

senses: A freshman at various Scottish and continental universities.
ety: From French béjaune (“freshman”), from bec jaune (“yellow beak”), in allusion to young birds.
examples: They'd been at it, say and night, for four years – only to be shown up by a snivelling little wimp of a bejan.

senses: To clean, polish, or wash (something) by rubbing and scrubbing it vigorously, frequently with an abrasive or cleaning agent.
To remove debris and dirt (from something) by purging; to sweep along or off by a current of water.
ety: From Middle English scǒuren (“to polish, scour; to clean; to beat, whip”), from Middle Dutch scuren, schuren (“to clean; to polish”) or Middle Low German schǖren, of uncertain origin but probably from Old French escurer, from Medieval Latin scūrō, escūrō, excūrō (“to clean off”), from ex- (“thoroughly”) + cūrō (“to arrange, see to, take care of”), from cūra (“care, concern”) (from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeys- (“to heed”)) + -ō. The word is cognate with Danish skure, Middle High German schüren, schiuren (modern German scheuern (“to scour, scrub; to chafe”)), Norwegian skura (“to scrub”), Swedish
examples: He scoured the burnt food from the pan.
There were the tawny rocks, like lions couchant, defying the ocean, whose waves incessantly dashed against and scoured them with vast quantities of gravel.

senses: A philosophy which holds that the universe is chaotic and irrational and that any attempt to impose order will ultimately fail.
Absurdity, something that is absurd
ety: From absurd + -ism (“doctrine, theory”).
examples: Henri Duval is a swashbuckling adventure with an absurdism straight out of Douglas Fairbanks: Siegel makes his hero a dandy who draws swords on men who insult his clothes.

senses: spicy soup or stew made from such leaves.
ety: From American Spanish calalú. Compare Sranan Tongo krarun, Dutch klaroen.
examples: But a little callaloo soup and a few mouthfuls of stewed goat, saw me much improved.

senses: A person, especially a woman, who frequently seduces men
ety: Blend of man + womanizer.
examples: If the Apocalyptic Aphrodisiac were to come, men would become womanizers, women would become manizers, and our ability to defend ourselves as a nation would crumble.

Blue was not as good a 'womanizer' as the rest of us, (surrounded, as we were, by 'manizers,') but he was a great guy to run into for a drink and a story, and a good friend and observer of the rest of us.

Worse yet, they could be stuck raising offspring with a man they despise. I have met some women in their forties recently that I could tag as “manizers.” Still, they are not nearly as ruthless as womanizers are.

senses: To allow a sauce or flavoring mixture to absorb into something; to steep or soak something in a marinade to flavor or prepare it for cooking.
To allow a substance to be absobed into the hair or scalp.
Of a substance, to absorb into the hair or scalp.
Of ideas or feelings, to mentally develop over time.
Especially of a haircut, to settle in and for one to get used to it.
ety: First attested in 1645; adapted from either French mariner or the earlier attested Italian marinare (“to pickle, marinate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from Late Latin marina (“brine, salt water”), short for aqua marina (“sea water”), from Latin marinus (“marine, of the sea”), from Latin mare (“the sea”) from Proto-Indo-European *móri (“the sea”).
examples: You'll get a better flavour from the chicken if you marinate it first.
After the chicken has marinated for two hours, discard the remaining marinade.
Let your scalp marinate while you shave.

senses: A French dessert made by baking fresh fruit (traditionally cherries) with a batter.
ety: Unadapted borrowing from French clafoutis.
examples: My clafoutis are not very sweet, and I enjoy them for breakfast as well as for dessert.

senses: A periwinkle or its shell, of family Littorinidae.
ety: Ellipsis of periwinkle.
examples: Shrimps and winkles are the staple commodities of the afternoon trade, which lasts from three to half-past five in the evening. These articles are generally bought by the working-classes for their tea.
Sometimes late at night men would come in with a pail of winkles they had bought cheap, and share them out.
Briony was on her knees, trying to put her arms round Lola and gather her to her, but the body was bony and unyielding, wrapped tight about itself like a seashell. A winkle.

senses: To move under the force of gravity.
To tend or drift towards someone or something, as though being pulled by gravity.
ety: Borrowed from New Latin gravitāt-, past participial stem of gravitō.
examples: Children naturally gravitate to such a big, friendly man.
The guests slowly gravitated to the kitchen.
The natural price, therefore, is, as it were, the central price, to which the prices of all commodities are continually gravitating.

senses: The moment in the plot of a drama in which the hero makes a discovery that explains previously unexplained events or situations; a denouement.
ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀναγνώρισις (anagnṓrisis), from ἀναγνωρίζειν (anagnōrízein, “to recognise, discover”).
examples: His heroines never have a true anagnorisis because the moral fault is never in themselves, only in outside conspirators.

senses: A beaten or pulverized mass.
An act of crushing or squeezing.
ety: Possibly blend of smash + mush.
examples: The steamroller left her pie an unrecognizable smush.

Some carriers are taking the smush to new heights. Spirit Airlines, for instance, uses seats on some flights with the backrest permanently set back three inches. Call it, as Spirit does, “prereclined.”

senses: A call-and-response chant performed in India's devotional traditions.
ety: From Sanskrit कीर्तन (kīrtana, “narrating”).
examples: She was not devout or overly religious but she went to temples and kirtans regularly.
Recently, Mrs. Breighner and Ms. Damon attended a Friday night kirtan at the Integral Yoga Institute.

senses: A representation of Japanese in Latin script.
ety: Transliteration from Japanese ローマ字(じ) (rōmaji, literally “Roman letters”).
examples: The romaji of the word ローマ字 is “rōmaji”.
The katakana and the hiragana are syllabic forms of writing derived from Chinese characters, while the romaji are the letters used in writing most European languages.
For example, in Japanese advertisements sexy and my house often appear in romaji, making the underlying concepts of eroticism and private ownership more exotic.

senses: A grandmother.
An elderly woman.
ety: Borrowed from Yiddish באָבע (bobe, “grandmother”), and then either from a Slavic language or from eastern Middle High German bābe (“old woman”), both from Proto-Slavic *baba (“old woman”) and ultimately imitative of a child’s babbling. Doublet of baba.
examples: I dedicate this book to my late grandparents, Morris and Bala Baellow. My bubbe’s inability to write in English turned out to be a blessing: she pressed me into service as her scribe at an early age.
Once, when I poked my stick in a bed of brown leaves, I found a shimmery snakeskin. When I showed my bubbe, she said I had found a memory of the snake, and that memories were precious.

senses: A Japanese business practice of continuous improvement in performance and productivity.
Continuous improvement generally.
ety: From Japanese 改善 (kaizen かいぜん), from Middle Chinese 改善 (kój-dʒjén) (compare Mandarin gǎishàn 改善), from Old Chinese 改善 (*qˁəʔ-ɡenʔ "to correct errors"), from 改 ("to change") + 善 ("good"). Introduced to English in 1959 by Boyé Lafayette De Mente in his book Japanese Etiquette and Ethics in Business.
examples: This is a big mistake, because Japanese railways were largely built using British equipment and technology. But what they have done since is ruthlessly improve and refine it, using Kaizen principles.

senses: Feathery; puffy, light, airy or windswept.
Elaborate, frilly, fussy or overwrought in a silly or purely decorative way.
Fluttery; emotional, worked up, especially over inconsequentials.
ety: Blend of fluffy + poofy.
examples: A well-prepared bed can supply asparagus for years and years. Then comes the bonus— in the fall, the wispy stems called “fern” become a blaze of yellow, floofy, feathery stems.
She'd always been stuck with naturally curly hair, but now the loose springy curls were doing whatever they wanted.To her, it was starting to look hopelessly floofy.
Do you love birds with floofy, profuse feathering?

senses: To wither or waste away.
To cause to waste away or become abortive; to starve or weaken.
ety: Borrowed from French atrophie, from Latin atrophia, from Ancient Greek ἀτροφία (atrophía, “a wasting away”), from ἄτροφος (átrophos, “ill-fed, un-nourished”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + τροφή (trophḗ, “nourishment”), from τρέφω (tréphō, “to fatten”). Equivalent to a- + -trophy.
examples: Boy. I love summer vacation. I can feel my brain beginning to atrophy already.
Cold silence has a tendency to atrophy any sense of compassion

senses: A curve or arc, especially in architecture or in the design of a ship.
The arc of smaller radius at the springing of an elliptical or many-centred arch.
ety: Anglo-Norman, from Old French haulce.
examples: He wears a minimal white cotton brief, and is pleased by the hance of its pouch, a catenary dip as he faces the mirror, the profile navicular and ostent.

senses: Giving rise to myths; pertaining to the creation of myth.
ety: From Hellenistic Ancient Greek μυθοποιία (muthopoiía, “mythopoeia”) + -ic.
examples: No other fully historical hero has furnished such a perfect opportunity for the mythopoeic faculty.
If we study myth in a scientific way, we miss the experience of moving into a mythopoeic mode of consciousness.

senses: The philosophical belief that prioritizes happiness, particularly sensual pleasure as the highest good in life.
A general devotion to the pursuit of pleasure.
ety: From Ancient Greek ἡδονή (hēdonḗ, “pleasure”) + English -ism. First attested in 1856.
examples: It began with his shrugging off of both family and faith and taking the Amtrak Vermonter out of Penn Station to major in minor hedonism and minor in the major modernists at a hippie college in the great Jewless north.

senses: A ghost, an apparition.
Spirit (of a group, age, era, etc).
ety: From German Geist (“spirit, ghost, mind”). Doublet of ghost.
examples: The geists eat and drink, but only as geists — not as spirits. ' We have dined,' they say ' sumptuously.' A vapour- ... If dead men tell no tales, their geists will tell them, if they find opportunity.
Koerg was not slow to recognize a geist; his knees shook, and he dared not utter a word.
The population that today explodes on a stagnant society with a catastrophic echo, is the geist of the times that shock our great nation into a new sense of her grandeur.

senses: The state or condition of being parallel; agreement in direction, tendency, or character.
The state of being in agreement or similarity; resemblance, correspondence, analogy.
A parallel position; the relation of parallels.
The doctrine that matter and mind do not causally interact but that physiological events in the brain or body nonetheless occur simultaneously with matching events in the mind.
ety: From parallel + -ism and from Late Latin parallelismus.
examples: Plutarch (c. AD 46-120), in his Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans, traced a parallelism between the most eminent men of the two countries.

senses: The wife of a German elector, often used as a title.
ety: From elector + -ess.
examples: The Electress Magdalena Sybilla was a woman of character, virtuous, kind, conventional and managing.
In July 1697 Electress Sophie had given an informal party for Peter which was attended only by her immediate family and the electresses of Brunswick and Hanover.

senses: A hybrid berry created from crossing blackberry, red raspberry, and loganberry.
ety: From Boysen + berry, named after its creator Rudolph Boysen.
examples: Like all caneberries, boysenberries are an etaerio or aggregate fruit containing several drupelets.
As mesmerizing as it is to watch Kristen Kish whip up bacon and cinnamon waffles with boysenberry and strawberry jam, imagine playing poker with Hosea Rosenberg.

senses: A sweet pastry found in many cuisines of the Middle East and the Balkans, made of chopped nuts layered with phyllo pastry.
ety: Borrowed from Turkish baklava, from Ottoman Turkish باقلوا (baklava) (see for more); possibly from Middle Mongol ᠪᠠᠭᠯᠠᠭ᠎ᠠ (baɣlaɣ-a, “bundle, package”).
examples: It meant lifting tea towels off trays in her Muslim neighbours’ kitchens to help herself to sticky triangles of baklava, half lemon slices pressed into the syrupy pastry filled with walnuts and raisins.

senses: A blanket, especially one used as a security blanket.
ety: Shortened from blanket + -ie.
examples: They instead sought out a place of refuge, somewhere familiar with a blankie and a mug of hot cocoa.

senses: A person whose profession is to create documentary films.
A person who writes software documentation.
A person who cares about communication and documentation.
ety: From documentary + -an. From document + -arian.
examples: After you have gone through all these steps, you are ready to tackle your company's documentation problems. You have also become an experienced systems documentarian...
Have you considered hiring a technical writer or documentarian to assist in the production of user manuals?

senses: Acting as the trusted recipient of a deposit.
ety: Borrowed from Late Latin dēpositārius.
examples: The hospital was the depositary institution of our monies.

senses: A small fragment or share of something, commonly applied to food.
A mouthful of food.
A very small amount.
ety: From Middle English morsel, from Old French morsel, from Medieval Latin morsellum (“a bit, a little piece”), diminutive of Latin morsum (“a bit”), neuter of morsus, perfect passive participle of mordeo (“to bite”). Compare French morceau, whence the English doublet morceau.
examples: By sticking out his tongue and curling it sideways to explore the hairy jungle around his mouth, he was always able to find a tasty morsel here and there to nibble on.
If a morsel of food fell off your plate, the advice of one contemporary document was to pick it up, make the sign of the cross over it, season it well - and then eat it.
Didn't even a morsel of decency remain in his brother?

senses: A modest, small, or trifling amount.
ety: From Middle English modicum, from Latin modicum (“a little, a small amount”), a noun use of the neuter form of modicus (“moderate; restrained, temperate; reasonable”) + -cum (suffix forming neuter nouns). Modicus is derived from modus (“a measure; a bound, limit”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *med- (“to measure”)) + -icus (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives). The plural form modica is derived from Latin modica.
examples: Unable to garner even a modicum of support for his plan, he conceded to follow the others.
There he lay quiet and composed, sipping small modicums of brandy and water, and taking his outlook into such transtygian world as he had fashioned for himself in his dull imagination.
I have learned from experience that a modicum of snuff can be most efficacious.

senses: One who, or that which, sizzles.
An Indian dish of meat and vegetables served sizzling on a hot plate.
A very hot day.
ety: From sizzle + -er.
examples: Today's a real sizzler, so it would be wise to put on sunscreen.

senses: The lifestyle, values, dispositions and expectations of particular social groups that are acquired through the activities and experiences of everyday life.
The liturgical clothing of monks, nuns and the clerical community, metaphorically referring to the religious mode of life.
ety: From Latin habitus (“habit”), from habeō (“have; maintain”). The plural habiti is a misconstruction, as the Latin plural is in fact habitūs. habiti may have been influenced by Latin habitī, the plural of the participle habitus; however, it is not the etymon of the English term.
examples: A wrestler could gain the rank of ōzeki based on his competitive achievements, but the promotion to yokozuna implied the presence of a certain habitus than embodied the quintessential traditional Japaneseness.
